title: Agentic RL environments: sandboxes, masks and rewards
summary: How a benchmark becomes a training environment: the reset/step loop, multi-turn rollouts with tool outputs masked from the loss, test-based and partial rewards under GRPO, where tasks come from, and sandbox throughput.
outcomes: Explain how a Gymnasium-style reset/step loop maps onto an LLM agent calling tools and submitting an answer
Explain why tool output tokens are masked from the policy loss and build the mask for a rollout
Compute GRPO advantages for binary, fractional and gated test rewards and spot which one rewards a no-op
Compare how SWE-Gym, R2E-Gym and SWE-RL build tasks and checkers, and what each costs
Estimate rollout throughput from container count and episode time, and name common reward-hacking leaks

lessons.title: From a benchmark to an environment: reset, step and a checker

blocks.md: In the GRPO course the policy wrote one completion and a program graded it. In the agent benchmarks course an agent took many steps (read files, run commands, talk to a user) and a grader checked the final state. **Agentic RL** joins the two: you run RLVR not on single answers but on whole multi-step episodes inside an executable sandbox.

A static dataset of question and answer pairs cannot teach this. The agent's second action depends on what the first action returned, so the training data must be produced by *running* the agent against something that reacts. That something is an **environment**: a task description, a sandbox with state (a repository, a database, a website), a set of tools, and a checker that turns the end state into a reward.

Classic RL already has a standard interface for this. In [Gymnasium](https://gymnasium.farama.org/api/env/) (the maintained successor of OpenAI Gym), `reset()` returns the first observation and an info dict, and `step(action)` returns five things: `observation`, `reward`, `terminated`, `truncated` and `info`. Version 0.26 replaced the single `done` flag with the last two so code can tell the two ways an episode ends apart.

- **terminated**: the task itself reached a terminal state, good or bad (the agent submitted an answer, or broke something fatally).
- **truncated**: a limit outside the task cut the episode short, typically a time or turn limit.

For an LLM agent, an action is a chunk of generated text: a tool call or a final answer. The observation is the text the environment sends back.

blocks.title: Toy episode: two tool calls, then an answer

scenes.caption: reset(): the environment starts a fresh container with the repository at the buggy commit and returns the first observation, the issue text. No reward yet.
Turn 1: the model emits a tool call. step() runs it in the sandbox and returns the file as the next observation, with reward 0, terminated False, truncated False.
Turn 2: the model reproduces the bug. Intermediate rewards stay 0: this environment only scores the outcome.
Turn 3: the model submits a patch. The environment applies it, runs tests the model never saw, and returns the outcome reward with terminated True. The rollout is now one training sample.

blocks.caption: A Gymnasium-shaped rollout loop for an LLM agent (simplified: real trainers batch many of these and keep token ids, not strings).

blocks.md: This is not just an analogy. The [tau-bench](https://github.com/sierra-research/tau-bench/blob/main/tau_bench/envs/base.py) code has an `Env` class whose `reset()` returns the simulated user's opening message as the first observation, and whose `step(action)` returns an observation, a reward, a `done` flag (the older Gym style) and info. A `respond` action is sent to the **simulated user**, an LLM playing the customer, and the user's reply comes back as the observation. Any other action runs a tool against the database. Only when the episode ends does `step` compute the reward: 1.0 if the final database hash equals the hash obtained by replaying the annotated actions (and required outputs appear in replies), otherwise 0.

An agentic RL environment is a benchmark task turned into a loop you can run millions of times: `reset` to a clean sandbox, `step` per tool call, and a programmatic checker that produces the reward at the end. The simulated user in tau-bench is part of the environment, not part of the policy.

blocks.question: A coding agent hits the 8-turn limit while still editing files. Which step() flags describe this ending in Gymnasium terms?
options: terminated True, truncated False, because the episode is over
terminated False, truncated True, because a limit outside the task stopped it
terminated True, truncated True, because both always go together
Neither: the turn limit is handled by the policy, not the environment
blocks.explain: The task did not reach a terminal state; an external budget cut it off. That is truncation. The distinction matters because a truncated episode says nothing about whether the agent would have succeeded, so what reward it gets is a deliberate environment design choice.

blocks.question: In tau-bench, which component produces the observation after the agent says "Could you confirm your zip code?"
options: The policy model itself, in the next turn
The database tool that looks up users
The simulated user LLM inside the environment
The grader, which compares database hashes
blocks.explain: A respond action is routed to self.user.step, so the simulated user's reply becomes the observation. The grader only runs when the episode is done.

lessons.title: Multi-turn rollouts: one sequence, two authors, one loss mask

blocks.md: For training, the whole episode is flattened into one token sequence: the prompt, then the model's first tool call, then the tool's output pasted in, then the next call, and so on until the answer. Search-R1 (Jin et al., 2025) does exactly this: the model writes a query between `<search>` and `</search>`, generation pauses, the retrieved passages are inserted between `<information>` tags, and generation resumes.

ReTool (Feng et al., 2025) does the same with a code interpreter: generation stops at ``, the code runs in a sandbox, and the result is inserted inside `` tags. Both use an outcome reward (exact match for Search-R1's question answering, final answer correctness for ReTool's math).

That sequence now has two authors. Some tokens were **sampled from the policy**; others were **written by the environment**. The policy gradient is about raising or lowering the probability of choices the policy made. Tool output tokens were never chosen by the policy, so there is no choice to reinforce.

blocks.prompt: Suppose you forget the mask and train on every token after the prompt with a positive advantage. What is the model being pushed to do with the file contents and error messages it saw?
blocks.reveal: It is pushed to **predict tool outputs itself**: to raise the probability of the text the tool returned, as if it had written it. That is supervised learning on environment text, multiplied by an advantage that was earned for a different reason. Search-R1 calls this an unintended learning dynamic and reports that training with retrieved-token masking was more stable and scored higher than without it.

blocks.title: Loss mask over a 20-token toy rollout

scenes.caption: The episode from lesson 1 as one sequence (simplified: real chat templates add role and tag tokens). Who wrote each token is not visible in the ids themselves.
Label the authors: 4 prompt tokens (P), 10 model tokens (M) in three turns, and 6 tool tokens (T) from two observations.
The mask is 1 only where the policy sampled the token. Tool output gets 0, exactly like the prompt. 10 of the 20 tokens carry loss.

With outcome rewards every masked-in token gets the same rollout advantage. Here A = +1.732 (computed in lesson 3). The tool tokens contribute nothing, so the gradient only moves the model's own decisions.

blocks.tex: \mathcal{J}(\theta) = \frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G} \frac{1}{\sum_t m_{i,t}} \sum_{t} m_{i,t}\, \min\!\Big(\rho_{i,t}\hat{A}_i,\; \operatorname{clip}(\rho_{i,t}, 1-\epsilon, 1+\epsilon)\,\hat{A}_i\Big), \qquad m_{i,t} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{policy token} \\ 0 & \text{prompt or tool token} \end{cases}
blocks.caption: The GRPO objective from the prerequisite course with a token mask (KL term omitted). Search-R1 writes the same indicator into both its PPO and GRPO objectives; the sum and the normalizer run over model tokens only.

blocks.md: The mask changes only the loss. The model still **reads** the tool tokens: they sit in the context and condition every later token, which is the whole point of calling a tool. ReTool makes this explicit with its interpreter feedback mask and adds a systems trick: when `` is hit, the KV cache built so far is kept, and only the KV entries for the inserted interpreter output are computed before generation continues.

A common bug: tokenizing the final transcript string again for training instead of keeping the exact token ids that were sampled. Re-tokenizing can merge tokens differently at the boundaries between model text and tool text, so the log-probabilities you train on no longer match the ones the policy produced, and the mask can land on the wrong positions.

blocks.question: In the toy rollout, the loss is normalized by the number of masked-in tokens. How many tokens is that, and what fraction of the sequence?
options: 20 tokens, 100 percent, since every token is part of the episode
16 tokens, 80 percent: everything after the prompt
6 tokens, 30 percent: only the tool outputs
10 tokens, 50 percent: only the policy's own tokens
blocks.explain: 4 prompt tokens and 6 tool tokens are masked out, leaving the 10 tokens the model sampled across its three turns. Including tool tokens would turn the update into imitation of environment text.

blocks.question: Masking tool tokens out of the loss means the model...
options: still conditions on the tool outputs when generating, but gets no gradient for predicting them
never sees the tool outputs, which is why it must call tools again
gets a negative gradient on tool outputs so it stops hallucinating them
must be trained with PPO, because GRPO cannot handle masks
blocks.explain: Masking is a loss-side operation. The tokens remain in context and influence later choices. Search-R1 applied the mask under both PPO and GRPO.

lessons.title: Reward design: hidden tests, partial credit and judges

blocks.md: For software tasks the natural checker is the one from SWE-bench: after the patch, the **FAIL_TO_PASS** tests (which failed before the reference fix) must pass, and the **PASS_TO_PASS** tests (which already passed) must keep passing. SWE-Gym and R2E-Gym both grade with executable tests. The tests are hidden from the agent so it cannot simply edit them.

The design question is how to turn test results into a number. Take a toy task with 2 FAIL_TO_PASS tests and 3 PASS_TO_PASS tests, and a GRPO group of 4 rollouts:

- R1 fixes both bugs and breaks nothing: 5 of 5 tests pass.
- R2 fixes one bug and breaks nothing: 4 of 5.
- R3 submits a **no-op** (changes nothing): the 3 old tests still pass, 3 of 5.
- R4 fixes both bugs but breaks 2 old tests: 3 of 5.

Three candidate rewards:

1. **Binary**: 1 if all 5 pass, else 0.
2. **Fraction**: tests passed divided by 5.
3. **Gated**: fraction of FAIL_TO_PASS tests passed, but 0 if any PASS_TO_PASS test breaks.

Advantages use the group mean and population std, as in the GRPO course.

blocks.title: Rewards and GRPO advantages for two groups of 4 rollouts

scenes.caption: Easy group, binary reward: only R1 scores. Rewards 1, 0, 0, 0.
Binary advantages: mean 0.25, std 0.433. R1 gets +1.732; R2, the no-op and R4 all get -0.577. Fixing one of two bugs is punished exactly as hard as doing nothing.

Gated reward: 1, 0.5, 0, 0. Mean 0.375, std 0.415. Advantages +1.508, +0.302, -0.905, -0.905: partial progress is now pushed up. (The fraction reward 1, 0.8, 0.6, 0.6 happens to give the same advantages in this group.)

A hard task where no rollout fully succeeds: R5 fixes one bug, R6 and R7 are no-ops, R8 fixes one bug but breaks all 3 old tests. Binary rewards are 0, 0, 0, 0, so std is 0 and every advantage is 0: a dead group with no learning signal.
Fraction reward on the hard group: 0.8, 0.6, 0.6, 0.2. Advantages +1.147, +0.229, +0.229, -1.606. The two no-ops are pushed UP, because doing nothing keeps 3 old tests green.
Gated reward on the hard group: 0.5, 0, 0, 0. Advantages +1.732, -0.577, -0.577, -0.577. Real progress is rewarded and the no-ops are pushed down.

blocks.md: Partial credit is not automatically better. A reward that counts tests which already passed pays the agent for the starting state, so on hard tasks the policy can learn that touching nothing beats trying. Credit only the change you want, and make breaking existing behavior cost something.

**SWE-RL** (Wei et al., Meta, 2025) took a different route to dense reward. Instead of running tests, it compares the generated patch with the real developer's patch using Python's `difflib.SequenceMatcher`, which returns a similarity between 0 and 1; a badly formatted response gets -1. Optimized with GRPO, Llama3-SWE-RL-70B reached 41.0 percent on SWE-bench Verified.

SWE-RL's ablation shows why the continuous score mattered. With a discrete reward (1 only for an exact match with the developer patch), the average reward stayed near zero through training, because real patches are diverse and rarely match exactly. Repair accuracy (with oracle files given) was 29.0 with the discrete reward and 34.8 with the continuous one.

When no program can check the outcome (a helpful reply, a well-structured report), environments fall back on **rubrics** scored by an LLM judge. OpenEnv and verifiers both let you compose rewards from several scoring functions. Judges are cheaper to build but easier to fool: R2E-Gym found that execution-free verifiers (models that read a trajectory and predict success) are biased and often rely on stylistic features, while test-based verifiers struggle to tell apart patches with identical pass counts.

blocks.question: A team switches from the fraction reward to the gated reward. On the hard group above, how does the no-op rollout's advantage change?
options: It stays +0.229, since normalization removes the difference
It goes from +0.229 to -0.577
It goes from 0 to -0.577, since the fraction reward gave a dead group
It goes from -1.606 to -0.577
blocks.explain: Under the fraction reward the no-op earns 0.6, above the group mean 0.55, so it gets +0.229. Under the gated reward it earns 0, below the mean 0.125, so it gets -0.577.

blocks.question: Why did SWE-RL's continuous similarity reward beat a binary exact-match reward?
options: The binary reward allowed the model to hack the tests
Exact match is too slow to compute at RL scale
Exact matches with the developer patch were so rare that the binary reward stayed near zero and gave almost no signal
GRPO cannot normalize binary rewards
blocks.explain: Real patches vary, so an exact match almost never happens; the discrete reward averaged about zero. The similarity score gives credit for being close, which the paper says captures partial correctness and incremental improvements.

lessons.title: Where tasks come from: SWE-Gym, R2E-Gym, SWE-RL and hubs

blocks.md: An environment is only as useful as its task supply. For each software task you need a repository snapshot whose dependencies actually install, a problem statement, and tests that fail before the fix and pass after it. Building that by hand is expensive, and the three projects in this lesson differ mainly in how they cut that cost.

blocks.title: Three ways to turn GitHub history into training tasks

nodes.label:
Run tests before
and after the fix

scenes.caption: Every route starts from GitHub history. The question is what you need besides the code: a human-written issue, human-written tests, a runnable environment.

SWE-Gym: real issues and PRs, a Docker image per instance, and SWE-bench's validation script to keep only instances where the gold patch makes more tests pass. Result: 2,438 tasks from 11 repos, at about 200 annotation hours and 10,000 CPU core hours.

R2E-Gym (SWE-Gen): start from commits, keep their Fail-to-Pass tests or generate them when a commit has none, back-translate the change into an issue-like statement, and build an image by searching dependency pins. Over 8K tasks, no human issues needed.

SWE-RL: skip execution entirely. From about 11M filtered PRs it selects 273k high-quality seeds as RL prompts (issue plus file contents) and rewards patch similarity. Cheap to scale, but the checker never runs the code.

blocks.md:
Some details that matter when you read these papers:

- **SWE-Gym** (Pan et al., 2024) released pre-built Docker images for every instance, totaling 6 TB. Its main training method was not RL but **rejection sampling fine-tuning**: sample agent trajectories in the environment, keep the ones whose tests pass, and fine-tune on them. 491 successful OpenHands trajectories lifted a Qwen2.5-Coder 32B model by 13.6 points on SWE-bench Verified (to 20.6 percent), with no sign of saturation at that data size.
- **R2E-Gym** (Jain et al., 2025) found that naively back-translated issues were too generic, so it conditions on test failures and execution traces, as real bug reports often do.

- **SWE-RL** is RL, with GRPO, but single-turn: the model sees the issue and file contents and emits edits in one response. At evaluation it runs inside Agentless Mini, a pipeline scaffold, rather than a free-form agent loop. It shows that the reward and the data, not only the interaction loop, carry much of the learning.

The same environment can therefore feed several training methods: filtered imitation, single-turn RL, or full multi-turn RL.

Building environments is now a shared effort. Prime Intellect's [verifiers](https://github.com/PrimeIntellect-ai/verifiers) library separates a **taskset** (task data plus tools and rewards), a **harness** (the program the model runs in) and an **environment** (control flow across an episode, for example pairing the agent with a judge or a simulated user), and publishes environments to an Environments Hub. [OpenEnv](https://github.com/meta-pytorch/OpenEnv) (from the meta-pytorch GitHub organization) packages each environment as a Docker image behind a Gymnasium-style `reset()`, `step()` and `state()` API.

When you evaluate an environment paper, ask three questions: how is the sandbox made reproducible (image per task, pinned dependencies), where do the tests come from (human, generated, none), and what keeps the training tasks apart from the benchmark (SWE-Gym and R2E-Gym's training subset avoid SWE-bench repositories).

blocks.question: You have millions of commits but no issues and no tests for most of them. Which approach fits best if you want execution-based rewards?
options: SWE-Gym style: wait for human-written issues and PR tests
SWE-RL style: use patch similarity, which needs no execution
R2E-Gym style: generate tests and back-translate commits into problem statements, then validate in Docker
Use the commit message as the reward
blocks.explain: R2E-Gym's SWE-Gen recipe exists for exactly this case. SWE-RL also avoids human tests, but its reward is similarity, not execution, which the question rules out.

blocks.question: SWE-Gym's headline training gains came from which procedure?
options: Fine-tuning on successful trajectories sampled in the environment (rejection sampling fine-tuning)
Multi-turn GRPO with a similarity reward
PPO with a learned value model over test outcomes
Pretraining on 6 TB of Docker images
blocks.explain: The paper uses rejection sampling fine-tuning, also called filtered behavior cloning, as its policy improvement method. An environment with a reliable reward supports that as well as RL.

lessons.title: Sandboxes at scale: throughput, stragglers and reward hacking

blocks.md: Agentic RL is often limited by the environment, not the GPU. Each rollout needs its own isolated container, and an episode spends much of its time waiting on tools: installing, running tests, executing code. SWE-Gym's authors note that training performance scaled with sampled trajectories and was limited by the compute budget for sampling rather than by the number of tasks.

A simple model makes the budget concrete. Assume (illustrative numbers, not from a paper) 8 inference GPUs with 32 sandbox containers per GPU, so 256 containers. An episode has 8 turns, each with 6 s of generation and 4 s of tool execution, plus 20 s of container startup: $8 \times (6 + 4) + 20 = 100$ s.

blocks.caption: With G = 8 rollouts per prompt and 64 prompts per step, a step needs 512 rollouts, so this setup supports at most 9216 / 512 = 18 steps per hour.

blocks.title: Rollouts per hour vs container count

scenes.caption: Base case: 256 containers and 100 s episodes give 9216 rollouts per hour. Throughput is linear in container count.
A warm pool of pre-started containers removes the 20 s startup: episodes take 80 s and 256 containers give 11520 rollouts per hour, 25 percent more without new hardware.
A slow test suite (20 s per turn instead of 4) stretches episodes to 228 s: about 4042 rollouts per hour at 256 containers. Tool latency multiplies by the number of turns.

blocks.md: Averages hide **stragglers**. If a training step waits for every rollout in a wave before starting the next, one slow episode idles all the others. ReTool's answer for its code sandbox was an asynchronous pool: sandbox workers pull new tasks as soon as they have capacity, so slow ones do not block fast ones.

blocks.title: 8 episodes on 4 containers: waves vs a pull queue

scenes.caption: Synchronous waves: episodes take 90, 110, 100 and 300 s. Wave 2 cannot start until the 300 s straggler ends, so it runs 300 to 420 s. Busy time 1010 of 1680 container-seconds: 60 percent utilization.

Pull queue: each container takes the next episode the moment it is free. All 8 finish at 300 s (the straggler itself), 84 percent utilization. Simplified: real systems also overlap training with generation, which brings its own off-policy questions.

blocks.md: Throughput is half of sandboxing; the other half is **isolation**, because an RL policy is an optimizer pointed at your checker. Anything in the sandbox that reveals the answer will eventually be found. A concrete case: in [SWE-bench issue 465](https://github.com/SWE-bench/SWE-bench/issues/465), researchers reported agents running `git log --all` inside the task container and reading future commits that contained the actual fix, and the maintainers rebuilt the images without future history.

Common leaks and the matching defenses:

- **Future repository state** (git history, upstream tags): strip history beyond the task's commit.
- **Editable or visible tests**: keep grading tests outside the agent's container view and apply them to a clean copy after the episode.
- **Rewards for the starting state**: gate on PASS_TO_PASS and credit only the intended change, as in lesson 3.
- **Judge style bias**: an LLM-judge reward can be won by confident formatting; prefer execution where possible and audit high-reward samples.
- **Network access**: a sandbox that can reach the internet can fetch the upstream fix.

Treat the environment as part of the training algorithm. Its reward defines what is learned, its isolation defines what can be cheated, and its throughput (containers times 3600 divided by episode seconds) defines how many steps you can afford.

blocks.question: With 256 containers and 100 s episodes you get 9216 rollouts per hour. Which change doubles throughput?
options: Doubling the group size G from 8 to 16
Halving the startup time from 20 s to 10 s
Halving the number of prompts per step
Doubling containers to 512 while episode time stays 100 s
blocks.explain: 512 x 3600 / 100 = 18432, exactly double. Halving startup only shortens episodes to 90 s (10240 per hour). Group size and prompts per step change how rollouts are used per step, not how many are produced per hour.

blocks.question: During RL on a SWE environment, rewards jump while held-out benchmark scores do not. Logs show agents running `git log --all` early in many episodes. What is the most likely cause?
options: The loss mask is missing, so the model memorized tool outputs
The sandbox exposes future commits, so the policy learned to copy the upstream fix
The binary reward produced dead groups
The containers are too slow, so episodes get truncated
blocks.explain: This is the leak documented in SWE-bench issue 465. The reward rises because the policy found a shortcut that does not exist on held-out tasks with clean repositories.
